result: ChIP-seq identified 4205 peaks for GFP::SMA-3 and 7065 peaks for SMA-9::GFP at the L2 larval stage in C. elegans. The GFP-tagged transgenes were validated as functional by their ability to rescue mutant phenotypes, and the L2 stage was chosen because it is when Smad reporter activity is high and body size differences first appear.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C68, C69, and C70 provide converging evidence for the ChIP-seq experimental design and results. The functional validation of the transgenes (C68) and the rationale for developmental stage selection (C69, C70) support the reliability of the ChIP-seq peak identification (C1, C2). The methodology is well-justified and the data are clearly reported.

result: SMA-3 and SMA-9 ChIP-seq peaks show substantial overlap, with 73.7% of SMA-3 peaks and 43.9% of SMA-9 peaks overlapping (3101 peaks total). The midpoint of inter-centroid distances was 788 bp (versus 8211 bp for randomized data), with ~45% of distances ≤100 bp, smaller than average peak sizes (400 bp for SMA-3, 250 bp for SMA-9), suggesting these factors frequently bind as complexes or in close proximity.
evaluation: Claims C3-C10 collectively demonstrate significant co-localization of SMA-3 and SMA-9 binding sites through multiple complementary analyses. The comparison to randomized data (C4) provides a critical control showing the observed proximity is non-random. The quantitative metrics (inter-centroid distances, peak sizes, overlap percentages) are internally consistent and support the interpretation of complex formation or close association (C8).

result: RNA-seq identified 1093 downregulated and 774 upregulated DEGs in sma-3 mutants, and 412 downregulated and 371 upregulated DEGs in sma-9 mutants (FDR≤0.05). Previously identified target genes (fat-6, zip-10) were detected, validating the approach.
evaluation: Claims C11-C14 report RNA-seq results with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR≤0.05). The validation through detection of previously known targets (C71) provides important confirmation of the experimental approach. The data are clearly quantified and referenced to supplementary files.

result: BETA analysis integrating ChIP-seq and RNA-seq identified 367 direct targets for SMA-3 and 332 for SMA-9. All SMA-3 direct targets were downregulated in mutants, indicating SMA-3 functions primarily as a transcriptional activator. In contrast, 46% of SMA-9 direct targets were upregulated and 53% downregulated in mutants, suggesting SMA-9 acts as either activator or repressor depending on genomic context.
evaluation: Claims C15-C21 describe the BETA analysis results and functional interpretations. The observation that all SMA-3 targets are downregulated (C17) strongly supports the activator function (C18). The mixed regulation by SMA-9 (C19, C20) appropriately leads to the dual function interpretation (C21). The integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq through BETA is methodologically sound for identifying direct targets.

result: LOA analysis identified 882 shared DEGs between sma-3 and sma-9 datasets. Combined BETA/LOA analysis identified 129 co-regulated direct target genes, of which 114 are activated by both factors and 15 show reversed regulation. For shared activated targets, loss of SMA-3 caused greater fold changes than loss of SMA-9.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 describe a sophisticated analytical approach combining LOA and BETA to identify co-regulated targets. The methodology addresses the limitation of arbitrary cutoffs (C22) and provides quantitative results (C23-C25). The observation about differential fold changes (C26) adds nuance to understanding the relative contributions of each factor. The approach is well-justified and results are clearly reported.

result: BETA/LOA analysis identified 238 SMA-3-exclusive and 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets. Of the SMA-9-exclusive targets, approximately half (129) are activated and half (150) are inhibited by SMA-9.
evaluation: Claims C27-C30 report the identification of factor-exclusive targets using the same BETA/LOA approach. The finding that SMA-9-exclusive targets show both activation and repression (C29, C30) is consistent with the dual function interpretation from C21. The numbers are clearly stated and internally consistent.

result: Less than 25% of all SMA-3 or SMA-9 sites were associated with HOT (High Occupancy Target) sites. Restricting to functional SMA-9 sites reduced HOT association to 15%, while 40% of co-regulated SMA-9 sites overlapping with SMA-3 were associated with HOT sites.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 address the important concern that many ChIP-seq peaks might represent non-specific binding at HOT sites. The analysis shows that most binding sites are not at HOT sites (C31), and functional sites show even lower HOT association (C32), supporting the biological relevance of the identified peaks. The higher HOT association for co-regulated sites (C33) is an interesting observation that warrants further investigation.

result: The sma-3; sma-9 double mutant showed an intermediate body size phenotype between the single mutants, rather than resembling one single mutant or showing an additive effect. This suggests SMA-9 may act as both a positive and negative regulator of body size, with some antagonistic activity toward SMA-3, partially suppressing the sma-3 small body size phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C34, C35, and C90 describe genetic interaction data that challenge simple epistasis models. The intermediate phenotype (C34) is clearly documented in Figure 4a, and the interpretation of dual positive/negative regulation (C35) is reasonable given this observation. This finding is important for understanding the complexity of SMA-9 function and is well-supported by the data.

result: For target genes showing opposite regulation by SMA-3 and SMA-9 (including C54E4.5, arrd-19, nspe-7, nspc-16, catp-3, and gdh-1), expression in the sma-3; sma-9 double mutant was not significantly different from the sma-9 single mutant, indicating the sma-9 loss-of-function phenotype is epistatic to sma-3 and that SMA-9 is required for SMA-3 to regulate these genes.
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 describe qRT-PCR validation of epistatic relationships at specific target genes. The observation that double mutants resemble sma-9 single mutants (C36, C38) supports the epistasis interpretation (C37). This is tested across multiple genes, strengthening the conclusion. The data are clearly presented in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

result: Gene Ontology analysis revealed both shared and unique functional enrichments. Shared targets included fatty acid metabolism, collagens, and one-carbon metabolism. SMA-3-exclusive targets were enriched for ribosome biogenesis, mitochondrial proteins, and ER chaperones. SMA-9-exclusive targets showed enrichment for oxidation-reduction/cytochrome P450s (activated) and innate immunity factors (repressed).
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 report GO term enrichment analysis results that provide biological context for the identified targets. The analysis reveals both convergent functions (C39) and factor-specific roles (C40-C42), which is consistent with the finding of both overlapping and exclusive targets. The enrichments are clearly reported with EASE scores in the figures.

result: Functional screening of target genes for body size effects identified 17 genes showing statistically significant body size reduction with Glass' effect size ≥1 in both wild-type and lon-2 backgrounds. Among individual mutants tested, only ins-7 showed significant reduction with effect size >1, while fat-6 and fat-7 mutants showed no significant difference from wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C43, C44, and C72 report systematic functional validation of target genes through body size measurements. The use of two genetic backgrounds (wild-type and lon-2) and Glass' effect size for normalization strengthens the analysis. The results are clearly quantified and provide important validation that these targets function downstream of the pathway. The data are presented in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

result: RNAi depletion of dpy-11 resulted in the most severe body size reduction among tested target genes. The dpy-11 gene encodes a protein-disulfide reductase involved in cuticle development, and its expression is regulated by SMA-3 but not by SMA-9.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 identify dpy-11 as a key downstream effector. The severe phenotype (C45) is clearly shown in Figure 5a and c. The gene function (C46) is appropriately cited to prior work (Ko and Chow, 2003). The differential regulation by SMA-3 but not SMA-9 (C47) is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5b and d.

result: While rol-6 mRNA levels are reduced in dbl-1 mutants at L2 (prior work), total ROL-6 protein levels are not significantly reduced in sma-3 or sma-9 mutants. However, cuticular ROL-6::wrmScarlet fluorescence was reduced in both mutants, and the protein accumulated intracellularly in the hypodermis rather than being properly secreted to the cuticle.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51 describe a key finding that the pathway regulates collagen secretion rather than just expression. The observation that total protein is not reduced (C49) but localization is altered (C50, C51) is well-documented in Figure 6d-g using the ROL-6::wrmScarlet reporter. This represents an important mechanistic insight beyond transcriptional regulation.

result: Super-resolution microscopy using an ER marker (VIT2ss::oxGFP::KDEL) showed that ROL-6 becomes trapped and accumulates at the hypodermal ER in sma-3 mutants. ER structures in sma-3 mutants were thinner with less complex and branched tubules compared to wild-type, consistent with a secretion defect.
evaluation: Claims C52 and C53 provide high-resolution cellular evidence for the secretion defect using structured illumination microscopy. The colocalization with an ER marker (C52, citing Tang et al., 2021 for the marker) and the altered ER morphology (C53) are clearly shown in Figure 7a-l. This provides strong mechanistic support for the secretion model.

result: Multiple perturbations of ER function phenocopied the BMP mutant secretion defects: RNAi of dpy-11, tunicamycin treatment (which inhibits glycan biosynthesis and ER secretion), and RNAi of ER-derived vesicle production/transport genes (C54H2.5, F41C3.4, Y25C1A.5, Y113G7A.3) all caused ROL-6::wrmScarlet accumulation in hypodermis and reduced cuticular deposition. Tunicamycin treatment also caused strong body size reduction.
evaluation: Claims C54-C58 provide multiple lines of evidence that ER secretion defects are sufficient to cause the observed phenotypes. The convergence of genetic (RNAi) and pharmacological (tunicamycin) perturbations all producing similar effects (C54, C55, C57) strongly supports the model. The body size effect of tunicamycin (C58) links ER function to growth. The data are shown in Figures 6h, 7m-n and supplementary figures.

result: The study concludes that DBL-1/BMP signaling promotes body size growth by promoting ER-specific processes involved in collagen maturation, transport, and secretion. SMA-3 and SMA-9 have both overlapping and unique target genes, with SMA-3 acting as a transcriptional activator and SMA-9 showing dual activator/repressor functions. Functional analysis revealed novel roles for one-carbon metabolism and ER secretory pathway genes (including dpy-11) in body size regulation.
evaluation: Claims C59, C92-C97 synthesize the major findings of the study. The conclusion about ER-mediated collagen secretion (C59, C96, C97) is well-supported by the ROL-6 localization studies, ER marker colocalization, and functional validation experiments. The characterization of overlapping/unique targets (C92) and differential transcriptional activities (C93, C94) is supported by the BETA/LOA analyses. The identification of one-carbon metabolism and ER pathway genes (C95, C96) is supported by GO analysis and functional screening. These represent the major conceptual advances of the work.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on TGF-β/BMP signaling, including the C. elegans DBL-1 pathway, Smad mechanisms, Schnurri homologs, and cuticle biology. This includes established facts about pathway components, signaling mechanisms, DNA binding specificities, and prior knowledge about SMA-9's context-dependent functions.
evaluation: Claims C60-C67, C79-C89, and C91 represent background knowledge appropriately cited to prior literature. These claims establish the scientific context for the current work and are well-supported by the cited references. They are not novel findings but provide necessary foundation for interpreting the new results.

result: The manuscript provides background on one-carbon metabolism (providing methyl groups for nucleotides, amino acids, glutathione, phospholipids, and epigenetic marks), collagen biology (role in body size and morphology), and prior examples of post-transcriptional regulation of collagens by DBL-1 signaling and TGF-β family members.
evaluation: Claims C73-C78 provide relevant background on metabolic and extracellular matrix biology that contextualizes the findings. These are established facts appropriately cited to prior literature (Clare et al., 2019; Page and Johnstone, 2007; McMahon et al., 2003; Fernando et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2018; MacFarlane et al., 2017). They support the biological significance of the identified target gene categories.
